name: Michelangelo
info: Michelangelo (1475–1564) was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect and poet of the High Renaissance, born in the Republic of Florence and active mostly in Rome, remembered for the Pietà, David, the Sistine Chapel frescoes and the dome of St Peter's.

facts.born: 6 March 1475 in Caprese, near Arezzo, Tuscany, as Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni; son of Ludovico, then the town's judicial administrator, from a Florentine family of small-scale bankers, and Francesca di Neri del Miniato di Siena
facts.died: 18 February 1564 in Rome, aged 88; his body was taken to the Basilica of Santa Croce in Florence, as he had asked, after a state funeral organised by Cosimo I de' Medici
facts.role: Sculptor, painter, architect and poet; architect of St Peter's Basilica from 1546
facts.known: the Pietà (St Peter's Basilica); the statue of David (1504); the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508–1512) and The Last Judgment (1534–1541); the Medici Chapel and the Laurentian Library; the tomb of Julius II, with its Moses; the design of the dome of St Peter's; more than three hundred sonnets and madrigals

t: Born in Caprese in 1475 and raised in Florence, Michelangelo was apprenticed to Domenico Ghirlandaio at 13 and joined the household of Lorenzo de' Medici, and he carved the Pietà and David before the age of 30.

For popes Julius II, Clement VII, Paul III and others he painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling and The Last Judgment and designed the Medici Chapel, the Laurentian Library and the plan of St Peter's, while the tomb of Julius II occupied him for forty years and was never finished to his satisfaction.

He was the first Western artist whose biography was published during his lifetime, and he also wrote more than three hundred poems, whose love for men later generations edited, allegorised or accepted at face value.
dyk: The Pietà is the only work known to have been signed by Michelangelo: his name is carved on Mary's sash.
ev: Born on 6 March in Caprese, near Arezzo
Apprenticed at 13 to Domenico Ghirlandaio in Florence
Completes the Pietà in Rome, at 24, and returns to Florence
Completes the statue of David, begun 40 years earlier by Agostino di Duccio
Finishes the Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted over about four years from 1508
Completes The Last Judgment on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, begun in 1534
Appointed architect of St Peter's Basilica at the age of 71
Dies in Rome on 18 February, aged 88; he is buried in Florence

sections.early:
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was born on 6 March 1475 in Caprese, a small town in Valtiberina near Arezzo. His family had for several generations been small-scale bankers in Florence, but the bank failed, and his father Ludovico briefly took a government post in Caprese, where he was the town's judicial administrator. His mother was Francesca di Neri del Miniato di Siena. The family claimed descent from the Countess Matilde di Canossa, a claim that remains unproven but which Michelangelo believed. The family returned to Florence a few months after his birth. After his mother's long illness and her death in 1481, when he was six, he lived with a nanny and her husband, a stonecutter, in Settignano, where his father owned a marble quarry and a small farm. There, according to his own words as Vasari quotes them, he received with his nurse's milk the knack of handling chisel and hammer.

He was sent to Florence to study grammar under the Humanist Francesco da Urbino but showed no interest, preferring to copy paintings from churches and to keep company with other painters. Florence was then Italy's greatest centre of the arts and learning, its art sponsored by the Signoria, the merchant guilds and patrons such as the Medici. He studied and copied in drawings the frescoes of Giotto and of Masaccio in the Brancacci Chapel.

In 1488, at 13, he was apprenticed to Domenico Ghirlandaio, who had the largest workshop in Florence. The next year his father persuaded Ghirlandaio to pay him as an artist, which was rare for someone so young.
sections.rise:
In 1489 Lorenzo de' Medici, the de facto ruler of Florence, asked Ghirlandaio for his two best pupils, and Ghirlandaio sent Michelangelo and Francesco Granacci. From 1490 to 1492 Michelangelo attended the Platonic Academy founded by the Medici, where Marsilio Ficino, Pico della Mirandola and Poliziano were among those who influenced his work and outlook. He carved the reliefs Madonna of the Stairs and Battle of the Centaurs, the latter on a theme suggested by Poliziano and commissioned by Lorenzo. At 17 he was struck on the nose by a fellow pupil, Pietro Torrigiano, which caused the disfigurement seen in his portraits.

Lorenzo's death on 8 April 1492 ended this security. Michelangelo went back to his father's house and carved a wooden Crucifix for the prior of Santo Spirito, whose hospital let him study anatomy on corpses, the first of several occasions in his career when he dissected. In 1494 the Medici were expelled from Florence with the rise of Savonarola, and he went to Venice and then Bologna, where he carved small figures for the Shrine of St Dominic. Back in Florence he carved a child St John the Baptist and a sleeping Cupid. According to Condivi, a Medici patron had the Cupid made to look buried so it could be passed off as ancient; the buyer, Cardinal Raffaele Riario, found out but was so impressed that he invited the artist to Rome. Michelangelo arrived there on 25 June 1496, aged 21.
sections.deeds:
In Rome he carved a Bacchus for Riario, which the cardinal rejected, and in 1497–98 was commissioned by the French ambassador, Cardinal Jean de Bilhères-Lagraulas, to carve a Pietà. He finished it at 24, and Vasari wrote that it was a miracle that a formless block of stone could be reduced to a perfection that nature can scarcely create in the flesh. Back in Florence in 1499, he completed the statue of David in 1504, a colossal marble figure begun 40 years before by Agostino di Duccio and intended as a symbol of Florentine freedom; a committee including Botticelli and Leonardo da Vinci placed it in the Piazza della Signoria.

In 1505 Pope Julius II commissioned a tomb to hold forty statues, to be finished in five years. Michelangelo kept being interrupted by other tasks, and worked on it for 40 years; its best-known figure is Moses, completed in 1516. In 1508 he began the Sistine Chapel ceiling. He had been asked to paint the twelve apostles; he persuaded the pope to give him a free hand and painted nine episodes from Genesis, with prophets and Sibyls on the pendentives. It covers more than 500 square metres and contains over 300 figures. It took about four years, to 1512.

From 1534 to October 1541 he painted The Last Judgment on the altar wall, for Clement VII and then Paul III. In 1546 he became architect of St Peter's and returned to Bramante's idea of a centrally planned church.
sections.opponents:
Michelangelo had hot-tempered quarrels with patrons. On 17 April 1506 he left Rome in secret after arguing with Julius II, and stayed in Florence until the Florentine government pressed him to go back. Condivi's account says that Bramante resented the tomb commission and persuaded the pope to give Michelangelo the ceiling, in a medium he did not know, hoping he would fail. In a letter of late 1542, Michelangelo himself blamed the tension with Julius II on the envy of Bramante and Raphael, saying of Raphael that all he had in art he got from him.

The Last Judgment drew objections. Showing Christ and the Virgin Mary naked was thought sacrilegious by Cardinal Carafa and Monsignor Sernini, who campaigned for the fresco to be removed or censored; Paul III resisted. Shortly before Michelangelo's death, the Council of Trent decided to cover the genitals, and Daniele da Volterra was commissioned to do so.

After the fall of the Florentine republic in 1530, where he had supported the republic and worked on its fortifications, Pope Clement, a Medici, sentenced Michelangelo to death; he was eventually pardoned. His biographer Paolo Giovio wrote that his nature was so rough and uncouth that his domestic habits were incredibly squalid and deprived posterity of pupils. His love poetry later troubled editors: his grandnephew published it in 1623 with the pronouns' gender changed, and the scholar Anthony Hughes argues that the poems to Tommaso dei Cavalieri cannot be taken as expressions of personal desire.
sections.last:
In 1527 the citizens, encouraged by the sack of Rome, threw out the Medici and restored the republic. A siege followed, and Michelangelo worked on the city's fortifications from 1528 to 1529. The city fell in 1530 and the Medici returned, with Alessandro de' Medici as first Duke of Florence. It is thought that Michelangelo hid for two months in a small chamber under the Medici chapels, drawing on the walls, in a room rediscovered in 1975. Pardoned, he left for Rome in 1534 and lived near Santa Maria di Loreto. There he met the poet Vittoria Colonna, who remained one of his closest friends until her death in 1547.

In his last decades he painted two frescoes in the Pauline Chapel, completed in 1550, and worked on architecture including the Campidoglio, the upper floor of the Palazzo Farnese and the Porta Pia. He wrote that painting and sculpture could no longer calm his soul, which had turned to divine love. He made Pietàs in old age, and the last sculpture he worked on, six days before his death, was the Rondanini Pietà, which he carved away until too little stone remained to finish it.

He died in Rome on 18 February 1564, aged 88. His body was taken to Santa Croce in Florence, as he had asked. Cosimo I de' Medici organised a state funeral and supplied the marble for his tomb, designed by Vasari for his heir Lionardo and taking over 14 years to build.
sections.legacy:
Michelangelo was the first Western artist whose biography was published during his lifetime. Vasari's Lives of 1550 gave him as its only living subject, presented his work as the culmination of the revival of the arts and called him divino. Condivi's Life of 1553, prepared with Michelangelo's participation, corrected Vasari in places. Contemporaries admired his terribilità, the ability to inspire awe. Vasari wrote that the Sistine ceiling had been a beacon to painters, restoring light to a world long in darkness. Attempts by later artists to imitate the expressive physicality of his style contributed to the rise of Mannerism.

His works influenced artists for generations. Raphael drew on his figures and prophets, Pontormo on the Last Judgment, and Rodin and Henry Moore on the unfinished Captives for Julius's tomb. The Laurentian Library vestibule was among the first buildings to use classical forms expressively; Nikolaus Pevsner saw in it Mannerism in its most sublime architectural form. The dome of St Peter's, completed after his death by Giacomo della Porta, influenced church building for centuries, including St Paul's Cathedral in London.

He was a devout Catholic, and enrolled in the Secular Franciscan Order. He lived simply, saying that he had always lived like a poor man, though his net worth was about 50,000 gold ducats. Since John Addington Symonds translated his poems in 1893 with their original genders, more readers accept that they express a preference for young men.

summary: Michelangelo (1475–1564), born in Caprese and raised in Florence, carved the Pietà and David before he was 30, painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling and The Last Judgment, and became architect of St Peter's at 71. He also wrote over three hundred poems.
references: Ascanio Condivi, The Life of Michelangelo (Pennsylvania State University Press, 1999)
Martin Gayford, Michelangelo: His Epic Life (Penguin Books, 2013)
James Ackerman, The Architecture of Michelangelo (University of Chicago Press, 1986)
William E. Wallace, Michelangelo: The Artist, the Man and his Times (Cambridge University Press, 2011)
notes: Dates: start 1475 and end 1564 as the article gives them, no hedge.
St Peter's: the article says he was appointed architect in 1546 (St Peter's section, and the key event) but 'took on the job' in 1547 (Architecture). The profile uses 1546 only.

Vittoria Colonna: the article says he met her in 1536 or 1538 in one place and puts her in Rome from 1534 in another; the profile says only that he met her in Rome and that she was a close friend until 1547.
Last Judgment: the article says Clement VII commissioned it shortly before his death in 1534; the profile says he painted it for Clement VII and then Paul III.

The article says the 1530 death sentence was lifted 'so that he could complete work on the Sistine Chapel and the Medici tomb'; the Sistine ceiling was finished in 1512, so that clause was left out. The profile gives the sentence after the fall of the city without stating a reason, as the article does.

Left out: the claim that Condivi downplayed his attraction to men and the Cavalieri correspondence's words, the Tommaso dei Cavalieri quotation, the Vasari quotation on the Pietà beyond the miracle line, Banister Fletcher's praise of the dome, BBC 'most famous statue', the popular culture list, and the Lomazzo anecdote about Raphael.
Statements about the Hughes view and the 1623 edition are given as the article gives them; the article says it is 'more accepted' since Symonds, not that it is settled.
Spellings kept British; 'organised' used for the article's 'organized'. References left empty for the editor.
